title: Astropedology

definition.text: The study of very ancient paleosols and meteorites relevant to the origin of life, and of soil systems on other planets.

facts.text: It is a branch of pedology concerned with soils of the distant geologic past and of other planetary bodies, to understand Earth's place in the universe.
If soil is a planetary surface altered in place by biological, chemical or physical processes, the question for Martian soils and paleosols becomes whether they were alive.
Better understanding of soil formation on other planetary bodies helped lead the Soil Science Society of America in 2017 to define soil as loose material altered at or near a planetary surface.
Astropedology symposia are a new focus of scientific meetings on soil science.
Paleopedology underpins both the study of ancient ecosystems on Earth and the emerging field of astropedology in exoplanet research.

distinct_from: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars

definition.text: The unconsolidated material covering the surface of the Moon, whose finer fraction is called lunar soil.

facts.text: Lunar soil usually means grains 1 cm across or less, and lunar dust the still finer fraction, under one millimetre.

It forms mainly by mechanical weathering, as impacts and charged solar and interstellar particles grind basaltic and anorthositic rock ever finer, unlike Earth's soil formation driven by oxygen, water and life.
Its density is about 1.5 g/cm³, rising with depth; by mass half is finer than 60–80 μm, 10% finer than 10 μm and 10% coarser than 1 mm.
Seven elements make up 98–99% of lunar rocks and soil: oxygen (41–45%), silicon, aluminium, calcium, iron, magnesium and titanium.
Its composition largely reflects the local bedrock: it divides into highland and mare regolith, and by ilmenite content into high-, low- and very low-titanium types.
Its main minerals include plagioclase, olivine and pyroxenes, with abundant impact-melt glass, and ice in permanently shaded craters.
Its fine particles are sharp, very adhesive and electrically charged, and reportedly taste and smell of spent gunpowder.
It could serve as a lunar resource, as building material such as lunarcrete and as a medium for growing plants.

conflicts.text: Lunar soil has a relatively low density of 0.9–1.1 g/cm³.
conflicts.note: Astropedology's range (printed '0-9-1.1') differs from the 1.5 g/cm³ given on Lunar regolith.

conflicts.text: Lunar dust is the fraction finer than 30 micrometres.
conflicts.note: The Regolith page's size limit for lunar dust differs from the under-one-millimetre limit on Lunar regolith.

definition.text: The making and continual alteration of lunar regolith by impacts and space radiation, known as space weathering.

facts.text: Its main processes are comminution by meteorite and micrometeorite impacts, agglutination of fragments by impact-melt glass, and solar wind sputtering and cosmic ray spallation.
Soils begin as a coarse, poorly sorted blanket of impact ejecta; micrometeoroids then grind it finer and add agglutinates and metallic iron, darkening it over time.
Soil forms far more slowly than on Earth: crater production rates suggest about 81 thousand years to overturn the top 2 cm.
Fire fountaining of lava also left glass-bead deposits, such as the orange soil at Shorty Crater found by Apollo 17 and Apollo 15's green glass.

title: Lunar dust hazards
article: Lunar regolith#Harmful effects of lunar dust

definition.text: The harm that fine, easily disturbed lunar dust can do to equipment and to the health of crews.

facts.text: It can darken surfaces and raise heat absorption, abrade materials by friction, and degrade seals, lenses, solar panels, windows and wiring.
Reactive particles in the lungs may cause respiratory disease, and long-term exposure possibly a disease similar to silicosis.
Apollo crews reported coughs, throat irritation, watery eyes and blurred vision from dust after moonwalks, though symptoms cleared within 24 hours.
A 2005 NASA study ranked dust the top challenge to study before a human Mars expedition, concerns that apply equally to lunar dust.

definition.text: The bringing of lunar rock and regolith back to Earth by space missions, beginning with Apollo.

facts.text: Apollo astronauts brought back some 360 kg of lunar rocks from six landing sites.
Every returned sample has been contaminated by Earth's air and humidity: the dust has rusted and lost its chemical reactivity, so it no longer matches conditions on the Moon.
On 16 December 2020 China's Chang'e 5 returned about 2 kg of lunar rock and soil, the first sample since 1972, making China the third country to do so.
Chang'e 6 returned samples from the far side of the Moon in 2024.

title: Martian paleosols

definition.text: Ancient soils on Mars, recognised from rover analyses and orbital remote sensing of the Martian surface.

facts.text: The Curiosity rover in Gale Crater found features like Earth's soil horizons and structures, including blocky angular peds, sand wedges, a shallow gypsic horizon and vesicular structure.
The Yellowknife Bay paleosols, about 3.7 billion years old, show olivine weathering to smectite and record a shift from possibly warm and wet to extremely cold and arid conditions.
Orbiters have detected phyllosilicate clays at thousands of sites dated to 4.0–3.7 Ga, explained either by hydrothermal activity or by surface weathering and pedogenesis.
Vesicular structures like those made by microbial gas in Earth's desert soils occur on Mars, but definitive evidence of life on Mars is still lacking.

distinct_from: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars

title: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars
article: Astropedology#Growing plants on the Moon and Mars

definition.text: Research into whether lunar and Martian soils, or simulants of them, can support the growth of plants.

facts.text: All essential plant minerals appear to be present in both soils in sufficient amounts, except possibly reactive nitrogen, which Mars Pathfinder could not detect.
Nitrogen-fixing species could make up the shortfall, but fixation needs atmospheric nitrogen, absent on the Moon and only a trace on Mars.
In a large controlled experiment, plants germinated and grew for 50 days on Mars and Moon soil simulants without added nutrients, doing much better on the Mars simulant.
Plants struggle in real lunar soil, so long missions may need imported Earth soil, chemically treated regolith or plants bred for it.

title: Archean paleosols

definition.text: Soils preserved from early Earth's Archean eon, which give circumstantial evidence of life in soils 3.42 to 3.46 billion years ago.

facts.text: Soil profiles from the Pilbara region of northwestern Australia show distinct depletion of phosphorus.
Sulfur bacteria commonly oxidise sulfur to sulfates such as gypsum and barite, minerals of today's acid sulfate soils and a possible reason for sulfate build-up in Archean paleosols.

distinct_from: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars

title: Origin of life in soil

definition.text: The idea that life evolved in soil, where water held between clay grains forms countless microscopic reaction chambers.

facts.text: These chambers may also promote the making of organic compounds by mechanisms shown in the Miller–Urey experiment.
Clayey and organic soils resist erosion and so keep producing clay and organic matter, and early unicellular life would also have bound the soil.
The weathering cycle still supplies the ingredients that life requires.

distinct_from: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars

definition.text: The fine blanket of loose, varied surface deposits covering Mars, whose finer fraction is called Martian soil.

facts.text: No samples have yet been returned to Earth; the soil has been studied remotely by rovers and orbiters.
Mars is covered with sand and dust and littered with rocks; fine dust lifted in planet-wide storms stays aloft and tints the sky reddish from rusted iron minerals.
Easily weathered olivine is still present, suggesting that physical rather than chemical weathering now dominates on Mars.
Water and carbon dioxide ices are thought to lie frozen in the regolith, and Mars Odyssey measured water content up to 5% by weight.
Ice-rich regolith is thought to speed soil creep, rounding the 'softened terrain' of the Martian midlatitudes.
In 2008 the Phoenix lander found the regolith basic, at pH 8.3, and containing nutrients such as magnesium, sodium, potassium and chloride.
In 2012 Curiosity's first X-ray diffraction of Martian regolith found feldspar, pyroxenes and olivine, resembling the weathered basaltic soils of Hawaiian volcanoes.
Research on Earth relies on simulants such as Exolith Lab's MGS-1, and planned sample-return missions beginning with Mars 2020 should allow more accurate ones.

title: Extraterrestrial soil definition

definition.text: The unsettled question of what counts as soil on other planetary bodies, where the usual Earth definition, which includes organic content, may not fit.

facts.text: Planetary scientists use a functional definition: rocks are fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles on the Wentworth scale, and soil is all other, typically loose material.
The planetary science community often adopts 'medium for plant growth', while a fuller definition calls soil altered surface material that records its environmental history and needs no life to form.
Under Earth systems many extraterrestrial soils would be Entisols in Soil Taxonomy or Regosols in the WRB, but applying Earth-based systems to such different settings is debatable.
An alternative would put all non-Earth soils in a new order or reference group, tentatively called Astrosols.

contested_note: Sources disagree on what soil means off Earth, from a medium for plant growth to any altered surface material, and on whether Earth classifications or a new Astrosol group should cover it.

definition.text: The chlorine-bearing perchlorate salts whose relatively high concentrations make Martian regolith toxic.

facts.text: NASA's Phoenix lander first found perchlorates, such as calcium perchlorate, on Mars in 2008; later landers and the Mars Odyssey orbiter showed they are spread across the planet.
Levels of around 0.5% in the regolith are considered toxic to humans, and even trace amounts interfere with human thyroid function.
In a 2013 study, 0.5 g per litre of perchlorate cut leaf chlorophyll, root oxidizing power and plant size, and the salts built up in the leaves.
The water hyacinth Eichhornia crassipes tolerated perchlorates and could help remove them, though the plants then held high concentrations.
Without an ozone layer, ultraviolet light reaches the surface and makes perchlorates more lethal to bacteria, and soil iron oxides and hydrogen peroxide add to their toxicity.
Some bacteria adapt to perchlorate or even live off it; a NASA-funded project from 2022 is studying Dehalococcoides mccartyi to break perchlorates into chlorides and oxygen.
Perchlorates may also make life-related organic molecules harder to detect.

conflicts.text: Perchlorate levels on Mars are 0.05 wt %.
conflicts.note: Astropedology's figure is a tenth of the 'around 0.5%' given on Martian regolith.

definition.text: The finest fraction of Martian regolith, under 30 micrometres across, much of it carried into the atmosphere.

facts.text: Atmospheric dust particles are generally about 3 μm across; dust from the 2001 global storms stayed aloft only 0.6 years, against about two years for Mount Pinatubo's.
On Earth soil moisture and oceans gather settled dust into larger particles, but neither works on Mars, so deposited dust is free to be lifted again.
Its composition, dominated by plagioclase feldspar and zeolite, suggests it is ground mechanically from basaltic rock with little chemical alteration.
A study found that it reacts with water to form highly reactive molecules like those that cause lung disease in quartz miners.

definition.text: An Earth material made to approximate the chemical, mechanical, engineering, mineralogical or particle-size properties of lunar regolith.

facts.text: Researchers use simulants to study handling, excavating, transporting and using lunar regolith, since real samples are scarce, small and contaminated by Earth's atmosphere.
Before Apollo, crushed Earth rocks stood in for lunar soil; some differed greatly from the real thing, and the Moon's pervasive sharp, fine dust came as a surprise.
Later simulants, such as MLS-1 and JSC-1, were split into highland and mare types made by crushing and sieving anorthosite or basalt, matched to returned Apollo and Luna samples.
JSC-1, developed by NASA and the Johnson Space Center in 1994 to approximate mare soil, came from a glass-rich basaltic ash.
The lunar scientist Larry Taylor criticised many simulants for poor quality control and money wasted on features with no documented purpose.
JSC-1A geopolymerises in alkaline solution into a rock-like material with compressive and flexural strength comparable to conventional cements.
Recent simulants include Exolith Lab's highland LHS-1 and mare LMS-1, and the Indian Space Research Organisation's highland LSS-ISAC1 for its Chandrayaan programme.

definition.text: The weathering of any object exposed to the harsh environment of outer space.

facts.text: Airless bodies such as the Moon, Mercury and asteroids are altered by cosmic rays, by solar wind irradiation, implantation and sputtering, and by meteorite and micrometeorite bombardment.
Much of what is known comes from lunar soils returned by Apollo, where impacts and particles comminute, melt, sputter and vaporize the soil.
Micrometeorite melt welds glass and mineral fragments into agglutinates, which make up as much as 60 to 70% of mature lunar soils.
Vaporised iron-bearing minerals such as olivine and pyroxene redeposit tiny blebs of metallic nanophase iron in agglutinates and thin grain rims.
As lunar soil matures it grows darker, redder and loses absorption-band depth, so young crater rays fade with time.
Understanding it is needed to interpret remotely sensed data from planetary surfaces.
It works more slowly on asteroids, yet soil grains returned by Hayabusa from Itokawa show definite space-weathering alteration.
Impacts on Mercury are expected to make 13.5 times the melt and 19.5 times the vapour per unit area as on the Moon.

definition.text: The stirring of the outer crust of airless moons and other bodies by impacts, called lunar gardening on the Moon.

facts.text: Lacking an atmosphere, such bodies have almost no erosion, so impact debris builds up at the surface as a rough soil, the regolith.
Later impacts, especially by micrometeorites, stir and mix this soil.
The top centimetre of the Moon was long thought to overturn every 10 million years, but a 2016 LRO study of impact ejecta put it closer to 80,000 years.

definition.text: An Earth material used to mimic the chemical and mechanical properties of Martian regolith for research and prototype testing.

facts.text: The first, JSC Mars-1, was made at NASA's Johnson Space Center in 1998 from palagonitic tephra, low-temperature-altered volcanic ash from Hawaii.
Mojave Mars Simulant (2007) was crushed basalt with minimal weathering, so unlike the clay-like JSC Mars-1 it did not attract water.
MGS-1 (from 2018), the first mineralogically accurate simulant, mixes pure minerals to match the Rocknest soil analysed by Curiosity in Gale crater.
No simulant includes the perchlorates Phoenix found in 2008, though users can add perchlorate salts; fine particles and crystalline silica pose some health risk.

definition.text: A proposed concrete-like building material made from lunar regolith to cut the cost of building on the Moon.

facts.text: Like concrete it would use aggregate, water and cement, with lunar regolith as aggregate and cement from calcium-rich lunar rock.
In 1986 Lin and colleagues made lunarcrete from 40 g of Apollo 16 regolith; it withstood 75 MPa of compression.
A waterless version binds regolith simulant with sulfur; a mix of 65% JSC-1 simulant and 35% sulfur averaged 33.8 MPa compressive strength.
AstroCrete, proposed for the Moon or Mars, binds regolith with human serum albumin from blood.

definition.text: The collection, processing and use of materials found on other bodies, such as the Moon or Mars, in place of materials brought from Earth.

facts.text: It could supply life support, propellants, construction materials and energy, reducing the payload launched from Earth.
Settling planets or moons will need local building materials such as regolith.
Water bound in regolith, ice or permafrost can be recovered by heating, though ice and permafrost may be harder than rock to mine.
Oxygen can be extracted from iron oxide in lunar regolith by heating it above 900 °C in hydrogen gas.

title: Viking lander biological experiments

definition.text: Four biological experiments carried to the surface of Mars by the two Viking landers in 1976 to look for signs of microbial life.

facts.text: Each lander used a robotic arm to put soil samples into sealed test chambers; Viking 1 worked near the equator and Viking 2 further north.
The gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer, sensitive to a few parts per billion, found no significant organic molecules; Martian soil held less carbon than lifeless Apollo lunar soil.
The gas exchange experiment fed nutrients and water to soil under helium; oxygen disappeared on contact with the soil and carbon dioxide kept evolving.
The pyrolytic release experiment exposed soil to carbon-14-labelled CO and CO2, then baked it at 650 °C to detect any carbon fixed as biomass.
Any positive result was to be checked by heat-sterilizing a duplicate sample: persisting activity meant chemistry, a lost response meant biology.
The general view is that the results are best explained by oxidative reactions with the soil, which constant ultraviolet exposure has given a thin layer of very strong oxidant.
Perchlorate, found by Phoenix in 2008, destroys organics on heating and yields chloromethane and dichloromethane, the very compounds Viking detected, so whether Viking found organics remains open.
A 2018 reanalysis of the GC-MS data suggested organic compounds may in fact have been detected, matching Curiosity rover data.

contested_note: Scientists still dispute whether the results reflect soil chemistry alone or could include biology.

title: Labeled release experiment

definition.text: A Viking life-detection test in which Martian soil was dosed with a dilute nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon-14 and the air above monitored for labelled gas.

facts.text: Both landers' first injections gave a steady stream of radioactive gas, from a sunlit surface sample and a sample from beneath a rock.
Samples heated 3 hours at 160 °C released no gas, and at 50 °C much less; but second and third nutrient doses released no more gas, unlike living terrestrial soil.
Superoxides formed by ultraviolet light, or hypochlorite from irradiated perchlorate, may explain the result chemically.
Its designer Gilbert Levin holds the positive results diagnostic of life, but most astrobiologists judge the experiments inconclusive or negative.

contested_note: Levin and Straat maintain the results indicate life; most astrobiologists attribute them to oxidizing soil chemistry.

definition.text: A proposed mission to collect rock and dust samples on Mars and bring them to Earth.

facts.text: Returned samples would allow far more extensive analysis than onboard sensors, focused on whether Mars once hosted life, and could be reanalysed by future instruments.
The Perseverance rover, landed in Jezero crater in February 2021, is caching rock, regolith (Martian soil) and atmosphere samples for return.
Back contamination of Earth by Martian organisms has been raised, but the scientific consensus is that the risk of large-scale effects is small.
Martian meteorites are another sample source: 356 had been identified by August 2023, out of over 79,000 known meteorites.

definition.text: The growing of plants in outer space, mostly in pressurized, weightless space gardens in low Earth orbit.

facts.text: The absence of gravity, important for root development, soil integration and watering, is the first challenge.
For long-term growth, nutrient supply to roots, biogeochemical cycles and microbial interactions in soil-based substrates are particularly complex.
In January 2019 cotton seeds sprouted in a sealed biosphere on the Chang'e 4 lander, the first plant grown on the Moon; it survived 2 days.
University of Florida tests showed Arabidopsis thaliana can germinate and grow in lunar soil, but slowly and with signs of stress.
